5973-thomas-wingfold-curate-v1:
George MacDonald begins the first volume with wind roaring in every chimney at once, drowning the moan and surge of the woods like a sea. Helen Lingard has stayed in all day, writing to her brother Leopold at Cambridge, and her planned walk in the park has slipped past luncheon into threatening haze.

She has never known a day's illness, and she fears wet weather little more than a young farmer does. Still she pauses at her window above shivering plants and looks out to garden and meadow. Its November weather and a spirited horsewoman set the tone for the curate's story.
frus-1872p2v1:
This volume prints the pleadings in the Alabama claims arbitration. It forms Part II, Volume I of the 1872 papers. The Treaty of Washington, signed May 8, 1871, created the Geneva tribunal. The American case opens the book. It charges Britain with unfriendly conduct through the war. Britain's case answers in its own block. An American counter case follows with a large appendix.

The evidence reaches beyond the cruisers themselves. Cuban correspondence from 1866 to 1871 fills one run. Spanish gunboats at New York get another. The monitors Catawba and Oneota appear at New Orleans. The Hornet and the Florida add further files. One law officers' opinion treats the Shenandoah at Melbourne. The volume is a courtroom in print. Two nations argue the war at law.
frus-1873p1v1:
Volume I of the 1873 papers is labeled general correspondence. It runs from the Argentine Republic to Mexico. China takes a long section, and Haiti a lively one. France, Germany, and Britain anchor the European side. Japan and Mexico close the list. Grant's message opens on an eventful year. A financial crisis has felled great fortunes, he reports.

The message also notes a capture on the high seas. A vessel under the American flag was seized, he says. The affair briefly threatened serious consequences. Vienna's exposition draws a brighter thread. American artisans and scientists went as commissioners. The correspondence itself stays mostly routine. Claims, posts, and ceremonies fill the year. Crisis frames the edges of a normal volume.
thomas-wingfold-curate-v1:
Volume one of George MacDonald's Thomas Wingfold, Curate begins with Helen Lingard watching a November storm from her window. Wind takes every chimney for an organ pipe, and woods moan like a sea. Helen delayed her park walk after writing a long letter to Leopold at Cambridge.

She is healthy, sensible, and seldom merry, yet weather and dress plainly affect her mood. The fireside grows more attractive as rain threatens outside. This record's opening is identical to the opening of the record named without a volume marker, so readers meet the same chapter twice in the library.
